Dancing to Wesley Tongson: Chris Wan Feng on Asia Society Hong Kong’s “UNARCHIVED”

On October 30, a rave took over the Chantal Miller Gallery at Asia Society Hong Kong Center (ASHK). “UNARCHIVED: Techno & Impermanent Flux,” organized by ASHK’s curatorial team in collaboration with Hong Kong artist Wai Pongyu, followed “Singing and Dancing with Brush and Ink: The Art of Wesley Tongson” (Jul 15–Oct 11), a comprehensive exhibition of works by the late Hong Kong ink painter (1957–2012). Drawing on the Wesley Tongson Archive at Asia Art Archive, the evening combined archival displays with sets by DJ Knopha and visuals by VJ Gerry Li.

Chris Wan Feng, the center’s head of gallery and exhibitions, spoke with ArtAsiaPacific about the archive’s limits, the risks of the format, and what the night left behind.

A rave at Asia Society is, by any measure, a historic gesture for an institution known for lectures and scholarly exhibitions. How did the idea arise, and what prompted so radical a leap from Wesley Tongson’s ink, conventionally read through stillness and discipline, to the dance floor?

I certainly did not expect to curate something like this at Asia Society so soon. The project emerged through a series of coincidences. While researching the history of the Asia Society Hong Kong Center building, we discovered references to underground parties held here in the 1980s and ’90s. That forgotten history immediately opened up different ways of thinking about the building.

Around the same time, preparing the Tongson retrospective led to the establishment of the Wesley Tongson Archive at Asia Art Archive. The artist Wai Pongyu was invited to engage with the materials, and our conversations soon moved beyond the exhibition. We both felt that Tongson’s late works, especially the landscapes he made with his fingers instead of a brush, contain extraordinary emotional intensity. They are often discussed in terms of spirituality and transcendence, but we also found vulnerability, urgency, desire, and perseverance. The idea of a rave emerged from that intuition—not as an illustration of the paintings but as a response to the emotional energy resonating within them.

The title “UNARCHIVED” implies resistance to the archive as a site of containment. What did you mean by “unarchiving,” and how does the rave recast the archive as a repertoire to be enacted rather than preserved?

Unarchiving does not mean rejecting the archive. It means returning it to life. Archives preserve traces but never life itself: documents, images, letters, and artworks survive, while emotions, relationships, and lived experience disappear.

I often return to the idea that all history is contemporary history. We never encounter the past directly, only through the questions we ask in the present. Every encounter with an archive involves projection, since we inevitably bring our own experiences, desires, and questions to the reading. Rather than pretend to recover an objective truth, I am more interested in making that process visible.

That is why “UNARCHIVED” was never only about Tongson. It was equally about what happened when Wai Pongyu encountered Tongson from the perspective of the present. The rave let us move from preservation to activation, as the archive entered sound, moving image, bodies, and space. In that sense, unarchiving is not about recovering the past but about allowing historical materials to re-enter the present.

Event documentation of “UNARCHIVED: Techno & Impermanent Flux” at Asia Society Hong Kong Center (ASHK), October 30, 2026. Photo by Ziv Wei. Courtesy ASHK.

Tongson’s ink retains traces of the gestures that made it, whereas a rave leaves only duration, sound, and bodies in motion. What did you gain, and what did you have to forfeit, in moving from a medium that fixes movement to one defined by its disappearance?

We gained not a new object but a new experience. A central idea of the project was to bring together two radically different forms of knowledge: the rational structure of the archive and the emotional intensity of the dance floor. Their encounter generated something that neither could produce on their own.

For me, the most valuable outcomes resisted documentation: unexpected conversations, emotional shifts, and the temporary communities that formed over a single evening. In trying to understand Tongson, we were forced to rethink ourselves, and the project became a process of self-discovery for everyone involved.

Painting offers permanence, while a rave vanishes almost as soon as it happens. But that disappearance creates its own experience, because what cannot be preserved demands presence. The things that cannot be fully archived are what matter most to me.

Ink painting is often framed as a solitary, meditative encounter, while the dance floor is collective and messy. Did you wish to resolve that tension between contemplation and immersion, or leave it productively unresolved?

We never intended to resolve that tension. In fact, we designed the project around it. Visitors arrived expecting a rave, but the first thing they encountered was an archive wall, showing materials from Tongson’s life, the retrospective, the building’s history, and the making of the project itself. At the same time, we agreed from the start that the rave had to be a real rave, not simply a representation of one.

The exhibition had closed, but we intentionally kept its traces in the space. Exhibition texts remained on the walls, display cases became archival installations, and lights once used for artworks illuminated the bar and its staff. Throughout the evening, some people danced, some read documents, and many moved between the two. For me, that coexistence was the work.

The program ranged from nostalgic pop to heavy techno. How did you, Wai Pongyu, DJ Knopha, and VJ Gerry Li translate Tongson’s rhythm and the exhibition title “singing and dancing” into sound and projection?

“Singing and Dancing” was one of our starting points. It comes from a seal in Tongson’s work, and we turned it into a badge for everyone who attended. Ink painting and techno seem far apart, but we were never interested in translating visual forms directly into sound. We were interested in translating intensity.

What fascinated us was that things separated by history, culture, geography, and medium can still resonate. The greater the distance between references, the more interesting the encounter. We also tend to forget that artists like Tongson were not only producers of culture but participants in it. Hong Kong’s New Ink movement developed alongside popular music, nightlife, cinema, and rapid modernization. So the question was never whether techno was faithful to Tongson. It was whether contemporary audiences could meet his work through a language that is still alive today.

Few institutions would risk this format. In designing the practical logistics of the event, how did you negotiate the institution’s duty of care and the rave’s demand for abandon?

Taking risks is necessary. Planning can reduce risk but never eliminate uncertainty, and projects like this are hard to grasp until they happen. I do not think duty of care begins with control. It begins with trust in participants, artists, and the possibilities of collective experience. Intensity and collective release are often mistaken for disorder, which I do not think is necessarily true. Looking back, trust may have been the most important material in the entire project.

The exhibition addressed Tongson’s struggles with mental health and his questioning of gender identity. Club culture has its own history as a refuge for marginalized communities. To what extent did you conceive the rave as a space of care and release connected to his biography?

One achievement of the retrospective was that it let us speak more openly about Tongson’s struggles with mental health and gender identity. But I did not want the rave to become a therapeutic narrative. The project may have started with Tongson, but it quickly moved beyond him. Every act of interpretation involves a degree of projection, and every attempt to understand another life is necessarily incomplete. We chose to acknowledge that rather than deny it.

If there was one feeling we hoped to create, it was not healing in any simple sense but an awareness of the present moment. If there was an act of care, it was not in providing answers but in creating space for vulnerability, uncertainty, and coexistence.

How did audiences respond, whether regular Asia Society visitors, the club crowd, or those who knew Tongson? What is the event’s legacy for Tongson’s reception and for how Hong Kong institutions might respond to an artist’s archive?

The response was overwhelming, and we received an unprecedented amount of support and feedback. From the beginning, we wanted the audience to be multiple and not a self-referential conversation within the art world. Art should speak to different people in different ways.

I also never expected everyone to have the same experience. What matters to me is that each person moves one step forward from where they began, whether through the archive or the party. Both are equally valid. This is an art project, but if someone simply had a great party, that is completely fine. I believe some of the deeper experiences we tried to create will stay with people in quieter, longer-lasting ways, and some may only reveal their significance much later.

On the night, I thanked everyone on social media and wrote, “We made history.” I don’t think that is an exaggeration. The project opened up a new possibility, showing that there are still many ways of thinking about archives, history, artistic encounters, and the future. More importantly, it reminded us that these conversations are still very much alive.

Michele Chan is managing editor at ArtAsiaPacific.
excerpt_original: The head of gallery and exhibitions gives an archive new life through an after-hours rave. Michele Chan

We invite you to enjoy and reflect on these works during this time."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Brassaï (1899-1984)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lovers Reflected In Mirror , 1932 © Estate of Brassaï/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Brassaï moved to Paris in 1924 and never left. He and that city just connected on a profound level and he made it his own even though he was technically an “outsider.” His objectivity and intelligence captured the nuances of the city from its streets to its cafes, its parks and monuments by day and night, and also its hidden secrets that no one had ever truly captured in such an insightful way before. More than anything, he understood human nature and the human psyche without judgement. This is one of the great images from his celebrated book, “The Secret Paris of the 30’s” and this print was formerly in the collection of one of the greatest 20th Century art dealers, Ileana Sonnabend, so we know the physical print is special."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Louis Stettner (1922-2016)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Elbowing Out of Town, News Stand, New York , 1954 © Estate of Louis Stettner/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Louis, in his 93 years, lived life to the fullest right until the end. He was for sure a Brooklyn boy, a true original character. To be in his presence was always amusing, engaging and insightful. This is one of my favorite images of his. I just devour newspapers and magazines but fear they will soon be a thing of the past, especially newsstands. So many of them have closed here in the last year. I just love the optimism emanating from this image. You know this young woman is going to have a great day. She is so focused and determined. Whether she is going on an audition or job interview, she is going to nail it for sure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mick Rock (1948)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lou Reed, “Transformer” , 1972 © Mick Rock/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I grew up loving and listening to all kinds of music from Bach to Puccini to Reggae to Jazz. I have always been energized by it and sometimes a single piece of music can encapsulate an era in which you lived. I certainly never lived in New York during the 1960’s and 1970’s as I was growing up in London, but through Lou Reed I can certainly imagine what it might have been like. Likewise a single image can evoke the same feeling. I was offered this print signed by both the photographer and the subject and had to have it to help me understand that era. One must never stop learning about things you know nothing about and this image helped me undertake that process."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Max Yavno (1911-1985)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Heiress, Carthay Circle, Los Angeles, CA, 1949 © Estate of Max Yavno/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Today is a special day. This is our 100th “Power of Photography” daily image. I cannot believe this number. How did this happen? This started out as a little self therapy over 100 days ago helping me get through the extraordinary times we are living in. Revisiting these images I had feverishly collected over 41 years brought back such great memories of how they had been acquired and the circumstances and the people involved. I thought I would do just a few and to my surprise the series developed its own momentum. Clients and friends forwarded them on to their families and friends and each day my colleagues Mike and David and I received heartfelt messages from all over the world from strangers telling us how these images have helped them navigate these surreal times and that they have given them hope for a brighter future which has been truly humbling."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I thought it would be appropriate today to feature the first photograph I ever bought all those years ago when I first arrived in California in 1979 to pursue my film making aspirations from London. Of course the image had a special autobiographical resonance for me as I had grown up obsessed with World Cinema. I struggled to find the $400 to pay for it and if I were sane I would have spent the money putting new brakes on the beat up Ford Pinto I was driving. But I guess fate had another career in mind for me and this single image you could say changed the direction of my life. I subsequently got to meet Max Yavno who was equally inspiring. Thank you Max."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I will try my best to continue this series and hope to present to you equally beautiful and soulful images. article_text:
Archives – October 20, 2020

This is the ninth installment of the online series by Peter Fetterman Gallery called the Power of Photography highlighting hope, peace and love in the world. We invite you to enjoy and reflect on these works during this time.

Brassaï (1899-1984)

Lovers Reflected In Mirror , 1932 © Estate of Brassaï/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery

Brassaï moved to Paris in 1924 and never left. He and that city just connected on a profound level and he made it his own even though he was technically an “outsider.” His objectivity and intelligence captured the nuances of the city from its streets to its cafes, its parks and monuments by day and night, and also its hidden secrets that no one had ever truly captured in such an insightful way before. More than anything, he understood human nature and the human psyche without judgement. This is one of the great images from his celebrated book, “The Secret Paris of the 30’s” and this print was formerly in the collection of one of the greatest 20th Century art dealers, Ileana Sonnabend, so we know the physical print is special.

Louis Stettner (1922-2016)

Elbowing Out of Town, News Stand, New York , 1954 © Estate of Louis Stettner/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery

Louis, in his 93 years, lived life to the fullest right until the end. He was for sure a Brooklyn boy, a true original character. To be in his presence was always amusing, engaging and insightful. This is one of my favorite images of his. I just devour newspapers and magazines but fear they will soon be a thing of the past, especially newsstands. So many of them have closed here in the last year. I just love the optimism emanating from this image. You know this young woman is going to have a great day. She is so focused and determined. Whether she is going on an audition or job interview, she is going to nail it for sure.

Mick Rock (1948)

Lou Reed, “Transformer” , 1972 © Mick Rock/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery

I grew up loving and listening to all kinds of music from Bach to Puccini to Reggae to Jazz. I have always been energized by it and sometimes a single piece of music can encapsulate an era in which you lived. I certainly never lived in New York during the 1960’s and 1970’s as I was growing up in London, but through Lou Reed I can certainly imagine what it might have been like. Likewise a single image can evoke the same feeling. I was offered this print signed by both the photographer and the subject and had to have it to help me understand that era. One must never stop learning about things you know nothing about and this image helped me undertake that process.

Max Yavno (1911-1985)

The Heiress, Carthay Circle, Los Angeles, CA, 1949 © Estate of Max Yavno/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery

Today is a special day. This is our 100th “Power of Photography” daily image. I cannot believe this number. How did this happen? This started out as a little self therapy over 100 days ago helping me get through the extraordinary times we are living in. Revisiting these images I had feverishly collected over 41 years brought back such great memories of how they had been acquired and the circumstances and the people involved. I thought I would do just a few and to my surprise the series developed its own momentum. Clients and friends forwarded them on to their families and friends and each day my colleagues Mike and David and I received heartfelt messages from all over the world from strangers telling us how these images have helped them navigate these surreal times and that they have given them hope for a brighter future which has been truly humbling.

I thought it would be appropriate today to feature the first photograph I ever bought all those years ago when I first arrived in California in 1979 to pursue my film making aspirations from London. Of course the image had a special autobiographical resonance for me as I had grown up obsessed with World Cinema. I struggled to find the $400 to pay for it and if I were sane I would have spent the money putting new brakes on the beat up Ford Pinto I was driving. But I guess fate had another career in mind for me and this single image you could say changed the direction of my life. I subsequently got to meet Max Yavno who was equally inspiring. Thank you Max.

I will try my best to continue this series and hope to present to you equally beautiful and soulful images. I appreciate all your support and encouraging words. Here’s to the next 100 days together. Be well, be safe.

Jürgen Schadeberg (1931)

Nelson Mandela in His Cell on Robben Island [Revisit] , 1994 © Estate of Jürgen Schadeberg/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery

This is one of the great images of history. It tells us so much of the human injustice of apartheid in a single frame. It has always moved me since the first time I saw it. I suggested to Jürgen that we should produce a special platinum print of it as I felt the process would bring out even more details of the human drama of the moment.. I find it tender and heartbreaking at the same time. It captures the soul of this special man whose words resonate with even more relevance today. “ Education is the most powerful weapon which you can use to change the world. ” ~ Nelson Mandela (1918-2013)

Yousuf Karsh (1908-2002)

Marx Brothers , 1946 © Estate of Yousuf Karsh/MFA Boston/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery

I grew up loving the Marx Brothers’ movies and whenever I need a pick-me-up I watch, “A Night at the Opera,” perhaps the funniest film ever made. As you dear friends can imagine we have all needed a lot of pick-me-ups recently… To my amazement a few years ago I came across this rare portrait of them by none other than one of my favorite portrait photographers, Yousuf Karsh. These genius comedians must have given Karsh, best known for his more serious studies of all the great statesmen, dignitaries and artists of the 20th Century, one of his most special sittings. Oh to have been a fly on the wall at this one.

Flor Garduño (1957)

Músico en la Nada, Escoma, Bolivia , 1990 © Flor Garduño/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery

Flor is one of my oldest photography friends. We were her first gallery and our careers have paralleled each other. Whenever we are together memories flood back for both of us. We laugh and sometimes cry and reminisce. And reflect on the passage of time and all we have been through, together and apart. Her great photographs are timeless and heartbreaking. None more so than this image, one of my favorites of hers. The subject is an itinerant Bolivian musician who travels through the country, playing at weddings and funerals and village events accompanied by all his worldly possessions. It has one on the most beautiful titles I have ever encountered.

Paul Caponigro (1932)

Backlit Sunflower, Winthrop, MA , 1965 © Paul Caponigro/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery

When you are in Paul’s presence you know you are in the presence of a special human being who exudes wisdom and insight. He is articulate and profound, but never pretentious. I see him as a kind of shaman, an elder who is a spiritual guide who has taught me much over all these years without ever pretending to be a teacher. I think his images work on a special plain of enlightenment. This is one of his great photographs. How can something so simple radiate so much power and beauty? As he tells the story, “A sunflower came as a gift from a friend and quietly took it’s place on my windowsill. It seemed content, as nature’s marvels usually are, with whatever notice it might receive. But as I passed it several times a day and glanced each time toward its radiance, the flower began to grow less shy. It seemed to ask, if not demand, that I draw nearer and record its moods on film. Finally I gave in and took the first step toward another world. As I dwelt upon the beauty of the sunflower, on its golden crown and everchanging form, it began to whisper of a realm beyond the sensual mind, a realm magnificent and strange.”

Bert Hardy (1913-1990)

Wartime Terminus, Paddington Station (Women Waving) , 1942 © Estate of Bert Hardy/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery

I love train stations and would much prefer to travel on them than any other form of transportation. They are great places also to view hellos and goodbyes. Here a mother is seeing her child off for safe evacuation to the English countryside from the perils of wartime London. So heart-breaking, but hopeful at the same time for a better future.

John F. Bullock

The Violinist , c. 1910 © Estate of John Bullock/Courtesy Peter Fetterman Gallery

John G. Bullock was a widely exhibited Pictorialist photographer in all leading salons at the turn of the century. He caught the eye of Alfred Steiglitz who included him in the Photo Secession’s inaugural exhibition of 1902 at National Arts Club in New York. His work is included in J. Paul Getty Museum, Metropolitan Museum and the Smithsonian Museu. This print is incredibly atmospheric and tender and inspiring. I have always thought of it like a great Mary Cassatt painting. The light streaming on her white dress and her focus. If it had been shot indoors it just wouldn’t have the same beautiful atmosphere and power.

Peter Fetterman

Peter Fetterman Gallery 2525 Michigan Ave, #A1 Santa Monica, CA 90404

article_text:
F or anyone remotely near the worlds of documentary, comedy or medical fraud, there has been one thing on the mind for weeks now: a single-minute clip of Nathan Fielder , the absurdist comedian whose boundary-pushing HBO series The Rehearsal cemented his status as docu-reality’s premier auteur, staring into the deep blue eyes of Elizabeth Holmes , the disgraced founder of the blood-testing startup Theranos. Unblinking, faces inches apart, the famously dry purveyor of harebrained business schemes and the convicted fraudster appeared locked in a battle of wills. “Are you being real right now?” Fielder asked her, in a classically meta bit – could Fielder really have spent years filming a secret documentary with one of Silicon Valley’s most notorious pariahs?

The prospect of TV’s grand illusionist versus emblematic girl-boss scammer seemed potentially too good to be true; buzz for You Can See Everything, Fielder’s furtive documentary co-directed with wunderkind du jour Lance Oppenheim (whose narrative feature debut, the Robert Pattinson-starring Primetime , premiered last month) was such that access to the film’s New York film festival premiere on Wednesday became this fall’s hottest ticket .

Those who were there can confirm: the hype is deserved. You Can See Everything is, somehow, more shocking, twistier, thornier and revealing than billed – a stupefying and gloriously destabilizing hall of psychological mirrors, a thrilling once-in-a-lifetime collision of director and subject. You know from the minute Billy Evans, Holmes’s shifty husband-cum-business partner who entered the picture post-Theranos, claims that “the best way for people to see who she is … is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”, while lying with Holmes on a playroom floor, that you’re in for a wild ride. My mouth was agape for, conservatively, one half of the film’s unusually deserved three-hour run time.

Let me say now, if you’ve made it this far: I will not spoil major shifts – and if you are at all familiar with the Fielder canon, you know they’re coming – for a singular movie whose enjoyment depends, in part, on an element of surprise, both for viewers and for film-makers who genuinely seem to not know what they signed up for when they walked into the Holmes-Evans household rental in 2023. Arguably the less you know about anything that is to come, the better.

What I can tell you is that You Can See Everything is a masterpiece of who’s playing who, the fragility and absurdities of trust, seemingly begotten by chance. Back in 2023, convicted of wire fraud and conspiracy and awaiting the start of her 11-year sentence in prison, Holmes, along with Evans – who appears to be her match made in heaven, as neither ever blink and are maybe always lying – sought out a film crew to document their life with their two young children, in an attempt to protest her innocence and, perhaps, rebrand for Theranos 2.0. For some reason, they chose Oppenheim, a documentarian whose distinctive style – hyper-saturation, tight frames, creeping zooms – exposes the eerie in the mundane, and Fielder, whose precise style of spectrum-y, extreme cringe means that no question will be off the table. As Fielder points out on camera, in one of several exquisitely blunt confrontations, it is an odd choice to allow a comedian famous for his business scams to make a documentary that will supposedly clear your name of arguably the most famous fraud scandal of the 2010s.

The result is a three-hour documentary filmed like a thriller and scored like a drama that plays like an unraveling of certainty in real time. Oppenheim’s house style, shots tightly hugging then boring into a face with laser-like curiosity, perfectly suits the material; scenes that could be an unlikely tableau instead become a fascinating parade of inscrutable motivations, isolated actors bristling against the others. There is something extremely satisfying in watching Fielder’s sharp angles – arched eyebrows, needling questions, dispensation of social buffers – tangle with Holmes’s disposition (or performance? or genuine personality?) of guileless warmth, a strange and compelling chemistry building within a reality distortion field. If Fielder’s earlier work felt at times like it was punching down, trading on the naivety of regular people, well, he has finally met his match.

I am, admittedly, writing around a film that must be seen to be discussed, and will surely engender much chatter as to what, exactly, we just witnessed. But trust that things devolve in a very Fielderian spiral, into a dissection of the form unlike anything I have ever seen or, as things get going and participants either lose their filters or sharpen their game, anything I have ever hoped to see when it comes to the figure known as Elizabeth Holmes . Trust, too, that if there was a question you were hoping to ask Holmes or, moreover, her husband – did he really have no reservations when he met the disgraced founder at a party in 2017, at the height of her scandal? – it gets asked, and then some (I did not need to know about conjugal visits, or lack thereof, in the Texas prison where Holmes continues to reside).

Trust, ultimately, that you can see more than you ever imagined you’d see about Elizabeth Holmes and maybe get no closer to discerning the truth – and yet it will all be worth it.

You Can See Everything screened at the New York film festival and will be released in the US on 16 October, in Australia on 12 November, and in the UK on 20 November

article_text:
T he giant wave’s foaming white summit spreads high over the heads of the helpless souls huddled in their long thin boats, crackling into what look like many sharp claws. It is a monster, hungry to swallow human flesh. But beyond it, over the wild water, soothing the terror of those in peril on the sea, is Mount Fuji – a solid cone of hope and solace. The mountain, not the wave, is the hero of this masterpiece, as it is the hero of all the prints in Dulwich Picture Gallery’s stunning exhibition – the first in Britain – of the complete Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.

When you look closely here at three different, superb impressions of Katsushika Hokusai’s Under the Wave off Kanagawa – widely known today as the Great Wave – your mental picture of this icon is shattered by the violent onrush of water. In reproductions the wave just seems beautiful, an elegant curl of blue and white. But here, to paraphrase Tennyson, it is nature, blue in tooth and claw. The wretched people are the emotional heart of the picture, their imminent risk of drowning its whole point.

The wave is out of control, murderous, yet it is also a passing moment, shows Hokusai, a devout Buddhist. He offers this consolation: the wave looks as vast as a mountain but soon it will break and be gone. Meanwhile the sacred peak of Mount Fuji endures eternally. It can’t be hurt by the ephemeral dragon of saltwater. Put your faith in the essential, enduring things beyond the nightmare of mutable appearances and you will find inner peace. The wave is an illusion. Mount Fuji is the truth.

Yet that colossal truth is easy to forget as we move around it, pass it by, catch sight of it in the everyday rush – a distant peak on the horizon. On a city bridge people swarm without looking up from under their round hats at the mountain in the distance. A man working bare-chested, wiry and worn, has no time to study the far-off peak as he concentrates on making a barrel.

Hokusai delights in epic shifts of perspective, seeing Mount Fuji as an apparently small insignificant object while filling the foreground with distracting action. You do a double take at Fuji from Kanaya on the Tōkaidō Highway. Dressed people sit on the shoulders of nude men who are almost completely submerged in turbulent blue and white water, while others are sealed inside boxlike palanquins to be carried too over the water by crushed bearers gasping for air. It is no illusion. This crossing point over the Ōi River was a key military point for the city of Edo, so no bridges were allowed to be built there. Travellers had to be borne across.

No one in this strange scene looks at Mount Fuji. And yet not to notice the mountain is to miss out on something very big indeed. In another image a ferryman does pay attention to it, set against a golden evening sky under a layer of deep blue, as he rows people across another river: some passengers also look, while others do not. Other people – tourists as well as pilgrims – seek out the views, like Hokusai himself, delighting in nature and its mystery, even in extreme conditions: one group has trekked to a country teahouse in winter to view Mount Fuji in the snow. They’re rewarded with an icy scene of devastating beauty, picked out in golden white and intense deep blue.

Hokusai’s miracle colour, Prussian blue, came from Europe, where it was first used in the early 18th century. His knowledge of perspective is also coloured by European art. But the traffic of influence went both ways. It is impossible to overstate the centrality of Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji to the birth of modernism. It is the first global masterpiece. When Hokusai created this series of closely linked prints in the early 1830s he reinvented landscape art as a conceptual and symbolic meditation that would thrill and inspire artists across the world.

It’s no secret that Van Gogh, Whistler and other members of the European avant garde collected and emulated Japanese woodblock prints. But I hadn’t realised how deeply Cézanne was in his debt: the French painter’s repeated efforts to paint Mont Sainte-Victoire in Provence, fragmenting its rocky mass into shards of perception to see its true nature and discover its secret, echo Hokusai’s journey around Mount Fuji. So do Monet’s obsessive paintings of Rouen Cathedral, a haystack and his (very Zen) waterlily garden. Hokusai taught these Frenchmen to see landscape as metaphysical.

That we make icons of separate images from this series – and not just the wave – is understandable. Here is Ejiri Station, Province of Suruga, Hokusai’s depiction of people holding on to their hats as the sky fills with blown paper in an unexpected turn in the weather. Jeff Wall famously restaged it in his photograph A Sudden Gust of Wind (After Hokusai) .

What a timeless artist Hokusai is, influencing Monet and Cézanne and still inspiring remakes today. But it distorts his meaning if we focus on his separate images without seeing them as part of one long meditation on Mount Fuji. By itself, Hokusai’s gust of wind may seem an image of crisis and impermanence. But Mount Fuji is in the background: the godlike summit that shows us there’s a serenity beyond the chaos.

title_original: Music Cinema Club : Joe la Panic n’a rien d’une “Créature moyenne”.
editorial_title_zh: Music Cinema Club：Joe la Panic 绝非“平庸生物”。
editorial_excerpt_zh: 凭借新单曲《Créature moyenne》——兼具数字迷醉与不眠之夜的氛围，这位年轻女歌手带来了一部具有宣泄意义的 MV，用真挚炽热的内省之旅取代了早期的忧郁。该 MV 目前正在所有 mk2 影院播映。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/cover-Creature-moyenne-1024x1024.jpg", "alt": "《Créature moyenne》封面", "caption": "", "credit": "Trois Couleurs", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这位拥有德克萨斯牛仔般名字的艺术家直到2021年才开始涉足音乐，今年她已发行了三首单曲：“chanson d’eau fraîche”、“tudum”和“créature moyenne”。这首最新的作品清新且充满冲动，在一部催眠般的 MV 中成型。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Copie-de-Capture-decran-2026-03-05-a-17.26.18-1024x568.png", "alt": "Copie de Capture decran 2026 03 05 a 17.26.18", "caption": "© YouTube 截图 / Joe la Panic", "credit": "Trois Couleurs", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "宛如一本私人日记，Joe 穿梭于都市丛林之中，镜头转换间，置身于巴黎地铁霓虹灯的光晕下，呈现出一种让人联想起王家卫的美学。我们跟随这位艺术家的漫步，看她孤身一人出现在车站的人群中，或是面部映在红色的交通灯光下，交替运用拼贴、快进和拖影效果（一种结合了慢快门和闪光灯的摄影技术），仿佛在将她脑海中的饱和感具象化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该 MV 的导演劳拉·布热尔（Laura Bougeard）和托马斯·阿兹纳尔（Thomas Aznar）恰如其分地展现了她带有讽刺与诗意色彩的乐句风格（她钟情于说唱念白，“我不是在刷手机，我是在抚摸它”）。Joe la Panic 的音乐极具个性，堪称其这一代人中锋芒毕露的笔触（这让人不禁想起 Miki，这位在2024年于 TikTok 上崭露头角的法韩双国籍艺术家）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "▌ 延伸阅读", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Miki：“保罗·托马斯·安德森是他那一代人中最伟大的天才”", "links": [{"text": "Miki : « Paul Thomas Anderson est le plus grand génie de sa génération »", "url": "https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/cinema/miki-regle-de-3/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "关注我们的社交平台", "translated": true}]

article_text:
L’artiste au nom de cow-boy texan qui n’a débuté la musique qu’en 2021, a sorti trois single cette année : “chanson d’eau fraîche”, “tudum” et “créature moyenne”. Ce dernier morceau, rafraîchissant et pulsionnel, prend forme dans un clip hypnotique.

Tel un journal intime, Joe sillonne la jungle urbaine, de plan en plan, sous les halos des néons du métro parisien, dans une esthétique qui évoque Wong Kar-wai. On suit l’artiste à mesure qu’elle déambule, apparaissant seule dans une foule de gare ou le visage à la lueur rouge d’un feu, alternant collages, accélérés et effets de shutter drag (technique de photographie qui combine un temps de pose lent et un éclair de flash), comme pour imager la saturation dans sa tête.

Laura Bougeard et Thomas Aznar, réalisateurs du clip, rendent justice à ses phrasés (elle aime les spoken words ) teintés de sarcasme et de poésie (“ Je scrolle pas mon tel j’le caresse” ). Du cachet, la musique de Joe la Panic n’en manque pas, s’imposant comme une plume incisive de sa génération (qui n’est pas sans rappeler Miki, l’artiste Franco-Coréenne révélée sur TikTok en 2024).

▌ À LIRE AUSSI

title_original: Cannes 2026 #9: Breaking Borders at Cannes Docs
editorial_title_zh: 戛纳2026第9期：在戛纳纪录片单元跨越边界
editorial_excerpt_zh: Jason Ryle、Mark Mushiva 和 Lisa Smith 讨论如何构建跨越国界、滋养彼此联系的电影网络。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "5月15日，《Film Comment》编辑 Devika Girish 在戛纳纪录片单元主持了一场专题讨论。该单元是专注于非虚构电影的行业平行单元。这场题为“跨越边界”的讨论探讨了一个问题：即使电影市场日益全球化，传统的专业网络与制作基础设施仍然围绕着关于国家与大洲的排他性观念而构建。Devika 邀请了三位领导开创性网络的嘉宾，他们正在推动跨国联系，不仅改变电影的版图，也改变我们对权力、地方与归属的理解。嘉宾包括北极原住民电影基金（Arctic Indigenous Film Fund）首席执行官 Jason Ryle、创意技术专家兼“法医建筑”（Forensic Architecture）研究员 Mark Mushiva，以及罗姆电影人网络（Romani Filmmakers Network）创始人之一 Lisa Smith。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "订阅《Film Comment》，即可阅读我们对2026年戛纳电影节的全部报道。", "links": [{"text": "Subscribe", "url": "https://www.filmcomment.com/subscribe"}], "translated": true}]

Titled “Breaking Borders,” the conversation examined how, even as the film market has become increasingly globalized, traditional professional networks and production infrastructure are still structured around exclusionary ideas about countries and continents. Devika gathered three panelists who lead groundbreaking networks that are nourishing connections across borders, changing not just the terrain of cinema but also of our notions of power, place, and belonging. The speakers included Jason Ryle, the Chief Executive Officer of the Arctic Indigenous Film Fund; Mark Mushiva, a creative technologist and Research Fellow with Forensic Architecture; and Lisa Smith, a founder of the Romani Filmmakers Network."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Subscribe today to Film Comment to catch up with all of our Cannes 2026 coverage.", "links": [{"text": "Subscribe", "url": "https://www.filmcomment.com/subscribe"}]}]
article_text:
On May 15, Film Comment Editor Devika Girish moderated a panel at Cannes Docs, an industry sidebar dedicated to nonfiction filmmaking. Titled “Breaking Borders,” the conversation examined how, even as the film market has become increasingly globalized, traditional professional networks and production infrastructure are still structured around exclusionary ideas about countries and continents. Devika gathered three panelists who lead groundbreaking networks that are nourishing connections across borders, changing not just the terrain of cinema but also of our notions of power, place, and belonging. The speakers included Jason Ryle, the Chief Executive Officer of the Arctic Indigenous Film Fund; Mark Mushiva, a creative technologist and Research Fellow with Forensic Architecture; and Lisa Smith, a founder of the Romani Filmmakers Network.

Subscribe today to Film Comment to catch up with all of our Cannes 2026 coverage.

1977 あの写真の私たち

劇場公開日： 2026年11月20日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

U-NEXTで 関連作品を見る PR

解説・あらすじ

台湾民主化運動の転機となった「中壢（ジョンリー）事件」を題材に、時代に翻弄された若者たちの切ない恋の行方を描いたドラマ。 1977年、戒厳令下の台湾ではフォークソング運動が盛り上がり、社会にはさまざまな緊張とエネルギーが渦巻いていた。保守的な客家の町・中壢（ジョンリー）にある華壢（ホワリー）写真館は、そんな時代の変化を静かに見つめ続けていた。主人の娘で読字障害を抱えるファン・シエンインは、小学校卒業後は進学せず、写真館を手伝いながら写真撮影を学んでいた。一方、彼女の幼馴染リー・ホングオは社会問題への関心が強く、大学に通いながらフォークソングの創作に参加している。ホングオは長年にわたり、シエンインに密かに恋心を抱いていた。ある日、韓国人のテコンドー指導者ジン・ハオシーが青年団に招かれ町にやってくる。過去に秘密を抱える彼の存在はシエンインの好奇心をかきたて、互いを知るにつれて3人の関係には微妙な変化が起こりはじめる。 ヒロインのファン・シエンイン役でNetflixドラマ「次の被害者」のムーン・リー、韓国人のテコンドー指導者ジン・ハオシー役で「あの夏、僕たちが好きだったソナへ」のジニョン、シエンインに密かに恋心を抱く幼馴染リー・ホングオ役で「離れて、離さないで」のエディソン・ソンが出演。
